explanations.explanation: Creditor it is, friend. That's a man her husband owed money to, and he's coming to take her two children as his slaves. She cries out to Elisha, the prophet of the LORD, with all of that on her shoulders. I can't imagine a heavier knock on the door.

No brother shows up in this verse, friend. The man coming is her husband's creditor, someone who is owed money. Family is who we expect to turn up when life gets hard, I think, so the guess makes sense. But here the knock on the door is a debt collector.

The neighbors don't come knocking in this verse, baker. They show up later, when Elisha, the prophet, sends her to borrow from them (2 Kings 4:3). The one coming to take her two children is her husband's creditor. Hold on to those neighbors, because they matter in a minute.

That's it, baker. She tells Elisha, the prophet, “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” One jar. When someone asks what you've got and the answer is that small, it takes some honesty to say it out loud. I'd have been tempted to dig around in the cabinets for something more impressive.

No coins in this house, friend. She says, “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” The word is nothing, except that one jar. Silver would have made her story a lot easier, and the text never mentions any.

No tools get mentioned, baker. The widow answers Elisha, the prophet, with “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” That's the whole inventory. Good thing she was honest, because that small jar is exactly where this story starts.

Empty jars, baker! Elisha, the prophet, tells her, “…borrow empty jars from all your neighbors.” Think about it. A woman with one jar of oil gets sent out to collect a pile of jars with nothing in them. I think that is a strange shopping list, and it makes you wonder what comes next.

Baskets don't hold oil very well, friend, and the text doesn't mention them anyway. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…borrow empty jars from all your neighbors.” Jars are what she's after. Remember that, because the story is about to fill them.

Lamps aren't on the list, baker. Elisha, the prophet, tells the widow, “…borrow empty jars from all your neighbors.” Jars, and empty ones. I can see why lamps came to mind, since lamps and oil go together in our heads, but the text says jars.

Close, but it's the opposite, friend. Elisha, the prophet, says it plain: “Do not gather just a few.” He wants lots of jars. Anybody who has ever grabbed one cookie box for a whole batch knows how that goes.

Right, baker, because Elisha, the prophet, says, “Do not gather just a few.” He sends her for empty jars from all her neighbors (2 Kings 4:3). So the plan was never to start small. He wants her collecting big.

True, friend. The text says, “When all the jars were full, she said to her son, ‘Bring me another.’” Only when there were no more jars did the oil stop flowing (2 Kings 4:6). Her sons kept bringing jars and she kept pouring. The oil lasted as long as the jars did.

It's true, baker, so this one was a trick. The oil didn't quit halfway. She kept pouring until all the jars were full, and she asked her son for another. Then he said there were no more jars, and the oil stopped flowing (2 Kings 4:6).

Debt is the first blank, friend. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt.” That's the very trouble she cried out about at the start, the creditor at the door. Now she has what she needs to settle it.

Remainder, baker! Elisha says, “Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” That means money is left over after the debt is paid. She came in worried about her sons being taken, and now Elisha says she and her sons can live on what's left.

No tithe in this verse, friend. Elisha says to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the remainder. The word he uses for what she pays is debt. I think tithe is a church word that came to mind, but it isn't here.

Harvest doesn't show up here, baker. It comes later in the chapter, when the boy goes out to his father with the harvesters (2 Kings 4:18). For the widow, Elisha says to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the remainder. The oil is the whole story in this part.

The neighbors helped by lending the jars, friend, but they're not the answer here. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” So the oil pays the debt, and what's left feeds her family. Nobody gets paid back in neighbors.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “So whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat.” Elisha, the prophet, kept coming back to the woman's house in Shunem. One meal turned into a habit.

False is right, baker. Verse 8 says, “…whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat.” Elisha, the prophet, became a regular at her table in Shunem. If I found a house where the table was always set, I'd start taking the long way home too.

A room, friend! She says, “Please let us make a small room upstairs and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him.” She says this to her husband after she sees that Elisha, the prophet, is a holy man of God. A bed and a table and a lamp. That's a thoughtful thing to give a guest.
No altar, baker. The woman asks her husband to make “a small room upstairs” (2 Kings 4:10). She wants a place for the holy man of God to stay. Bed, table, chair and lamp, so it's a guest room.

A storehouse is for storing, friend, and nobody is storing anything here. She asks for a small room upstairs with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp (2 Kings 4:10). It's for Elisha, the prophet, so he can stay when he comes to them.

It's the other way around, baker. Elisha, the prophet, is the one who offers, asking whether he can speak on her behalf to the king or the commander of the army. She doesn't ask for it. She simply answers, “I have a home among my own people.”

False, friend. Elisha, the prophet, is the one who makes the offer, asking whether he can speak on her behalf to the king or the commander of the army. Her reply is, “I have a home among my own people.” A word with the king would be a big thing to say no to, and she did it kindly.

explanations.answer: She has no son and an old husband
explanations.explanation: That's what Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says. His words are, “Well, she has no son,” and “her husband is old.” Elisha asked what should be done for her, and Gehazi had an answer ready. Sometimes the servant is the one who notices.

explanations.answer: Her fields have had no rain
explanations.explanation: Rain doesn't come up, friend. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “Well, she has no son,” and “her husband is old.” That's what he points out about her. Nothing about fields or weather.

explanations.answer: Her family owes a large debt
explanations.explanation: A debt was the widow's problem at the start of the chapter, baker, not this woman's. Here Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “Well, she has no son,” and “her husband is old.” Easy to mix up two women in one chapter. This one in Shunem has a different need.

explanations.answer: She asks him not to lie to her
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. She says, “No, my lord… Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” That's a woman who doesn't want to be handed hope that she can't hold. I think she was being careful with her heart. Notice, the text doesn't say why she answered this way.

explanations.answer: She laughs to herself about it
explanations.explanation: No laughing is recorded here, friend. What she says is, “No, my lord… Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” She speaks to Elisha, the prophet, right to his face. Plain words, not a private chuckle.

explanations.answer: She runs to tell her husband
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say she goes anywhere, baker. She stands in the doorway and says, “No, my lord… Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” That's her whole answer to Elisha, the prophet. The next thing we're told is that she conceived.

True, friend. Verse 17 says, “But the woman did conceive, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her.” Elisha, the prophet, had said it, and it happened on the schedule he gave. She had told him not to lie to her, and she wasn't lied to.

It happened, baker. The text says, “But the woman did conceive, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her.” Elisha, the prophet, said it, and it came true right on time. That's a whole year of waiting that ended in a baby.

His mother, baker. The father says to a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The boy had cried out, “My head! My head!” and his father sent him straight home. I think this is a hard moment, and I'll just say it plain.
No uncle in this story, friend. The father tells a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The boy has just cried out, “My head! My head!” His mother is the one the father wants him with.

A nurse isn't mentioned, baker. The father tells a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The boy had said, “My head! My head!” and the father's answer was to get him to his mother. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: On the man of God's bed
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The text says she “laid him on the bed of the man of God.” That's the bed in the upstairs room she and her husband had made for Elisha, the prophet. Then she shut the door and went out. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think she's holding it together by doing one step at a time.

Her own bed isn't where she puts him, baker. The text says she “laid him on the bed of the man of God.” That's the bed in the little upstairs room made for Elisha, the prophet. Then she shut the door and went out.

explanations.answer: In the field by his father
explanations.explanation: He's not back in the field, friend. His father was out there with the harvesters, and a servant carried the boy to his mother (2 Kings 4:19). She laid him “on the bed of the man of God.” That's in the room upstairs, and then she shut the door.

That's what she says, baker. Her husband asks why she's going today, since it's not a New Moon or a Sabbath, and she answers, “Everything is all right.” That's all the text tells us she says. Why she put it that way, the passage doesn't say.

She doesn't say that to him, friend. When her husband asks why she'd go to the man of God today, she answers, “Everything is all right.” The text gives us only those words. It's a hard moment to read, so I'll just stay quiet beside her for a second.

explanations.answer: The man of God sent for me
explanations.explanation: No one sent for her, baker. In the text she is the one who asks her husband for a servant and a donkey. When he asks why she'd go today, her answer is, “Everything is all right.” That's the whole reply.

explanations.answer: He tells Gehazi to leave her alone
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Elisha, the prophet, tells his servant Gehazi, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” Gehazi came to push her away, and Elisha stopped him. Elisha saw that she was hurting, and that mattered more than manners.

explanations.answer: He lets Gehazi lead her away
explanations.explanation: Elisha does the opposite, baker. He tells Gehazi, his servant, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” So she stays right at his feet. Gehazi was the one pushing, but Elisha made the call.

explanations.answer: He tells her to go home and wait
explanations.explanation: She doesn't get sent home, friend. Elisha, the prophet, says to Gehazi, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” She had ridden all that way to reach him. He lets her stay.
Not this time, baker. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” So he doesn't know yet what has happened. Even a prophet only knows what he's told.
False is right, friend. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” He knows her soul is in deep distress, but not why. That's why he lets her speak.

The staff, baker! Elisha tells Gehazi, his servant, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go!” Then Gehazi is to lay it on the boy's face. Tie up the garment, grab the staff, and move. That's a man with somewhere to be.

Cloak is a fair guess, friend, but the text says staff. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go!” Gehazi's garment is the one getting tied up. The staff is what he carries.
No ring in this one, baker. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go!” A staff is what he's handed. Rings stay out of this story.

It's the opposite, friend. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him.” No chatting on this trip. Think of the longest hello you've ever had with a neighbor, and picture skipping all of that.
Right, baker. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him.” No hellos in either direction. Just go.

That's what she says, friend. “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” She had already clung to his feet, and now she says it outright. So he got up and followed her.

She doesn't ride ahead, baker. She tells Elisha, the prophet, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” She stays with him. The text then says, “So he got up and followed her.”

Waiting isn't what she's after, friend. She says to Elisha, the prophet, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” She wants to stay with him. And he gets up and follows her.

True, baker. The text says, “…there was no sound or response.” Gehazi, Elisha's servant, went back to meet Elisha and told him, “The boy has not awakened.” This is a heavy moment, and I think it's okay to just sit with it.

It happened, friend. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, laid the staff on the boy's face, “but there was no sound or response.” Then he told Elisha, “The boy has not awakened.” This part of the story is heavy, and I think we can let it be.

He prays, baker. The text says Elisha, the prophet, “went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.” Before anything else happens, he talks to God. That's the order of things.

The text doesn't say he weeps, friend. It says Elisha, the prophet, “went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.” I think his heart was heavy, but that's my guess. What the text tells us is that he prayed.

There's no oil in this scene, baker. Elisha, the prophet, “went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.” The oil belonged to the widow's jars at the start of the chapter. Here he prays.

Warm, friend. The text says, “As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body became warm.” Elisha, the prophet, had stretched out on the bed over the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand. That's the first change we see.

It's the other direction, baker. The text says, “As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body became warm.” Elisha, the prophet, was on the bed over him when it happened. Warm is the first sign of change.
Not stiff, friend. The text says, “As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body became warm.” That's what happened as Elisha, the prophet, lay over him. Warmth was the first change.

explanations.answer: The boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says Elisha, the prophet, stretched himself out over the boy again, “and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” Seven times, and the text counts every one. After all that heaviness, I think this is the moment the room changes.

explanations.answer: The boy sits up and calls for his mother
explanations.explanation: The boy doesn't say a word in the text, friend. It says, “…the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” Elisha, the prophet, had stretched himself out over him a second time. Sneezes and open eyes, and we don't get anything more.

explanations.answer: The boy groans and asks for his father
explanations.explanation: No groaning in the text, baker, and he doesn't ask for anyone. It says, “…the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” That's after Elisha, the prophet, stretched himself out over him the second time. Those are the details we're given.

True, friend. The text says, “She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground.” Only then did she pick up her son and go out. I think that says a lot about her heart in that moment, and the text lets her do it without a word.

She did, baker. The text says, “She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.” The bowing comes first, and then she picks him up. It's quiet and it says plenty.
